finalResponse:
# Fourth Pass — Where the Work Happens

*Same house style. Two questions from the last brief are still unanswered and I've stopped raising them; I'd only observe that this one has the same shape — an operating decision being presented as a facilities decision — and I'll design for silence again.*

---

## The thing that is not being said

We are being asked about desks, remote days and collaboration tools. Underneath there are two decisions of a different order, and neither is on the agenda.

The first is compensation geography. Do we pay for the role or for the postcode? Every answer to "where can people work" is downstream of that, and if we settle the office question first we will have accidentally set a global pay policy by implication — the worst way to set one. Location-adjusted pay is entirely defensible right up to the moment we are bidding for the same engineer against a firm that doesn't adjust, at which point we discover we have chosen a talent strategy without discussing it.

The second is what we think flexibility is *for*. Access to labour markets we cannot otherwise reach, or square footage we no longer want to pay for? Those two goals produce nearly opposite designs. Cost wants consolidation and a rolled-up global rule. Talent wants divergence, patience and permanent small footprints in places that will never justify themselves on a floorplan. I can build either. I cannot build both while calling it one programme.

## Permissions don't travel. Defaults do.

Here is the failure I'd expect most, and it is cultural rather than legal.

Write a policy that says *employees may work remotely with manager agreement* and observe what happens. In some of our markets uptake will be near-total, because "may" is read as "can." In others it will be close to zero, because "may" is read as "not unless invited," and nobody wishes to be the person who asked. Within eighteen months we will have manufactured a two-tier company along national lines, and it will show up first in who gets promoted, then in exit interviews, and finally in a works council meeting.

So the design principle: state **defaults**, not permissions. "Two days on site, Tuesday and Wednesday, unless the team publishes a different pattern" is a sentence that means the same thing in Osaka, Munich and São Paulo. "Feel free to come in when it suits you" does not. Ambiguity is not generosity; it is a tax paid by whoever is most junior and least sure of their standing.

And the corollary — the thing seniors must actually do rather than announce: the default must be visibly used by the people who don't have to use it. A flexibility policy that senior leadership is exempt from is not a policy, it's a rumour.

## A floor, and then deliberate divergence

I would resist a global standard. Not on principle — because the variation is real, and because uniformity mostly serves reporting convenience.

The office means genuinely different things in different places. Where housing is dense and commutes are long, the office is a service to employees, not an imposition on them: it is quiet, air-conditioned, has a chair that isn't a bed. Where junior staff live with family until thirty, "work from home" can mean "work from a kitchen table with four other people in the room." Where domestic broadband is unreliable, remote-first is a policy that quietly rewards the wealthy. A single global rule will land as thoughtfulness in one country and as cost-cutting in the next.

So: a narrow floor, non-negotiable everywhere, and freedom above it.

The floor is short. A guaranteed overlap band per team, chosen by the team and published. Decisions recorded in writing in one canonical place, always, whether or not a meeting happened. A stated maximum on recurring synchronous hours. Home-working equipment and connectivity paid for by us, not absorbed as an invisible personal cost — the least glamorous line item and the one that determines whether flexibility is a benefit or a transfer of overhead onto salaries. Local statutory rights treated as the floor's floor: right-to-disconnect regimes, co-determination obligations, permanent-establishment exposure. In several jurisdictions we do not have the authority to announce this at all, only to negotiate it, and I'd rather we discovered that before the town hall than after.

Everything else — days, patterns, ceremonies, whether the office is a base or a destination — belongs to the team and the country. Then publish the divergences side by side and let them compete. Deliberate variation is how we learn what worked; the only party who needs one global model is whoever is preparing the slide.

## The cheapest work, done first, everywhere

Before a lease is signed or a platform is bought: cut the recurring meeting load, hard. Establish written-first defaults for decisions and status. Set overlap bands and let the rest of the day belong to the person living it. Rebuild onboarding for someone whose first ninety days are mostly on a screen. Make search work.

Ninety days, near-free, and it does something the property team and the software vendors will both dislike: it lowers the baseline. Much of what is currently attributed to *not being in the room* is a meeting culture that would fail in the room too. If hybrid only breaks when measured against an unreformed calendar, we have not been shown a problem with hybrid.

There's a second dividend, and it's the strongest argument in this document. Most of our people work in a language that isn't their first. Synchronous discussion in English systematically advantages the fluent and the loud; written, searchable, asynchronous work advantages the competent. Async is not a scheduling convenience for a global company. It is the single largest available intervention in who gets heard.

## What the office is now for

Not desks. Rooms.

A building full of individual workstations is a building optimised for the one activity that demonstrably does not require a building. The things that decay remotely are specific and mostly social: apprenticeship, tacit knowledge, weak ties, the early-career network a person builds in their first two years and lives off for twenty. Design for those and the space requirement changes shape entirely — fewer square metres, more enclosed rooms, better catering than we think is dignified, and a deliberate budget for gathering people who are not otherwise co-located.

Take space the way I'd take machinery: modular, short-dated, reversible. Flexible leases and serviced space where the case is close, because we will be wrong in at least three cities and I would like to be wrong cheaply. And keep a small presence in each key market even where the spreadsheet objects. Reopening is dramatically more expensive than staying.

## The trap

Flexibility over *place* is easy and cheap. Flexibility over *time* is what people actually want, and it's the one we'll quietly withdraw.

The mechanism is familiar: remove the commute, and the calendar expands into the space it left. Add a global time zone spread, and someone in Singapore or California is on calls at both ends of their day, permanently, without anyone ever deciding it. We will have granted location freedom and confiscated the day — and we'll be puzzled by the attrition, because on paper we were generous.

So the guardrails are about hours, not addresses: a hard cap on recurring synchronous time, rotation of the unsociable slot rather than permanent assignment to whichever region is politest about it, and no meeting that could have been a document. Measure it. Publish it by region.

## Never remove the fallback

The irreversibility here is asymmetric and it is not ours. A remote permission is consumed within weeks — people move city, move country, sign a lease, enrol a child in a school. Rescinding it later is not a policy change; it is a mass termination with better manners. So anything we grant, we grant knowing we cannot take it back, and we say the duration out loud at the point of granting. Relocation across borders in particular should be a deliberate, individually-papered decision, never a policy footnote — tax residency, social security, immigration status and our own permanent-establishment exposure all sit in that footnote.

And no reorganisation of physical footprint inside the two quarters after the announcement. Let the pattern stabilise before we buy or dispose of anything based on it.

## How we'd know

Promotion rate and pay-increase rate by days-on-site, by country, by tenure band, reviewed quarterly. This is the whole audit. Proximity bias is the failure mode of every hybrid company on earth and it is entirely visible in that one table. If the in-office cohort is advancing faster on equivalent performance, we have not built flexibility; we have built a slower track and staffed it with the people whose lives are least accommodating.

Then: regretted attrition by location and by manager, because this will be a manager-quality story wearing a real-estate costume. Time-to-competence for new hires, and specifically for early-career hires, which is where remote genuinely costs something. Internal mobility rates into and out of non-headquarters countries — the honest test of whether "global" means anything. Meeting hours per person and out-of-band hours per region. Cost per collaboration-day, not cost per square metre.

And one number I'd refuse to set: an occupancy or attendance target. Name it and it will be met — by badge-in, coffee, and departure, in offices full of people on video calls to other offices. We'll have bought the metric and lost the thing it was standing in for.

---

## What I'd resist

The single global policy document. The enterprise platform purchased as a substitute for deciding how we work. Badge data used as a performance signal, ever. The word "culture" deployed without a stated mechanism. Senior exemptions, spoken or observed. Any disposal of space justified by six months of post-announcement behaviour. And the executive who has already chosen the answer and would like a framework to arrive at it independently.

---

The pattern, once: this is a pay decision, a management-capability decision, and a decision about who gets promoted — with buildings and software arriving afterwards to ratify choices we'll have already made by other means.

Which leaves the two things I'd want and don't have: whether the objective is talent reach or property cost, and whether the compensation-geography question has already been settled somewhere I can't see. The second would make most of the above either obvious or unnecessary.

I'll assume, as before, that silence is an answer of a kind.
